title: Chapter 215 – What the Cut Gave Back
html:
[Hall of Ten Thousand Names – Yue]

Yue takes the stair three steps at a time, which is a thing she has not done since she was nineteen and had two good knees.

She does not think about the knees. She does not think about the old man who calls out behind her, or the guard who flattens against the wall, or the woman with the porridge bowl who sits down suddenly on the bottom step and does not get up. She thinks about a single sound: Mei's voice, rising through the vaulted dark of the Hall of Ten Thousand Names, saying her name in a pitch she has never heard it said.

She reaches the east alcove in nine breaths.

The curtain is torn down. The lamp has fallen and gone out and somebody has lit another, a cheap tallow stub, which gutters in a draft and throws the shadows about like thrown cloaks. Mei is on the bed with a bundle in her lap. The bundle is a child in a nightshirt. It is entirely, terribly still.

"She's cold," Mei says.

Yue crosses the room. She goes down on her knees at the bedside and puts two fingers under the child's jaw, and for a moment there is nothing, and she thinks, with the flat calm of the long-trained, so this is how it ends. Then there is a flicker. Faint. Wrong. A moth beating against a window.

"She's alive."

"I know she's alive. I can feel her." Mei's voice is thin and cracked. "I can feel all of her. I can feel her slipping. It's like holding water in a net."

"What did you do?"

"Nothing! I didn't—" Mei stops. She is shaking. In the poor light she looks younger than she has in months, a girl of nineteen with her hair coming loose and her sleeves torn at the cuff. "She lent me strength, Yue. In her sleep. For twelve days. She was giving me her own, so I wouldn't be so thin, and I didn't know, and the fault in her blood—"

"The Lin fault."

"It opened." Mei's eyes are enormous. "Every time. A little more. And I thought it was gone, I thought Jian cured it, but he only cured the sickness. The fault was always there. It was waiting."

Yue looks at the child.

She is perhaps seven years old. She has dark hair, plastered to a damp forehead, and a small, serious, sleeping face. She has Mei's mouth. She has, Yue sees with a sudden unwelcome clarity, Lena's. There is something in the set of the lips that is not Lin at all, and Yue, who has been a hard woman a long time, finds that her own throat has closed.

"What do you need?" she says.

"I don't know."

"Mei."

"I don't know," Mei whispers. "The Ring would have known. The Ring would have drawn it back. But the Ring's gone. It let Jian go. It let him go, and now I can't—"

She stops.

Her face changes.

---

It happens slowly.

Yue has seen a great many faces change in a great many rooms. She has seen a general realize he is outflanked. She has seen a mother realize her son will not wake. She has never, until this moment, seen a girl of nineteen realize that the worst thing that has ever happened to her is also, in some terrible and unexpected way, a door.

"It's gone," Mei says.

"What is?"

"The Ring." Her eyes go to some middle distance. "It was draining me. All the time. Every day, a little. I thought it was the Print, I thought it was the leak, I thought it was Jian's distance. It wasn't. It was the circle. It was holding the nine of us in step, and I was the weakest link, so I was the one who paid." She laughs, a short ugly sound. "It cut itself. It cut Jian loose because he was dragging the rest of us down, and now there's no circle, and the eight of us are—"

She puts her hand flat against her own breastbone.

"I'm full," she says. "Yue. I'm full."

"Full of what?"

"Everything I had. Everything the Ring took." She turns, wide-eyed. "My capacity. It's coming back. All the spare I lost, all the days, it's coming back to me like—like water into a dry well. I can feel it filling."

Yue stares at her.

"Can you give it to her?"

"What?"

"The child. Can you give it back?" Her own voice is sharp and level, a general's voice, the one she uses when she needs another person to stop being afraid. "She lent you strength. You owe her. Can you return it?"

Mei opens her mouth. Closes it.

"I don't know how," she says.

"Then find out."

---

It takes the whole of the night.

Yue stays for all of it, because she does not know how to leave. She sits on the end of the bed with her back to the wall and her knees drawn up and watches, in the dim tallow light, as Mei bends over the child and closes her eyes. Kuang comes at the second hour, and Hai Ren at the fourth, and between them they spread a blanket and fetch hot stones and say nothing. The old clerk's eyes are red and his shaking hand is folded over the head of his cane. He looks, Yue thinks, like a man waiting at a river for a boat he is not sure will come.

She does not know what Mei is doing. She is not a healer, and she has never pretended to be. What she can see is that the girl's breathing has gone shallow and slow, that a faint white sweat has broken on her brow, and that her hands, hovering above the child's chest, are shaking with the effort of not touching.

"Don't force it," Hai Ren says, softly. "It isn't a thing you do. It's a thing you let happen."

"I'm not forcing it."

"You're holding your breath."

Mei lets it out.

Something in the room shifts. There is no light, no sound; but Yue feels it as she feels a change in weather, a quickening of pressure, the first soft drop of rain on a roof. The child's fingers, curled on the blanket, loosen. The faintest color rises in her cheeks. And Mei, bent over her, makes a small broken sound and says, "There. There. She's taking it."

"Is it enough?"

"I think—" Mei's voice shakes. "I think I'm giving her all of it."

"All?"

"All of what I got back." She is crying now, quietly, without moving her hands. "I don't have to keep any. The Ring's gone. I don't need a spare. I only need—"

She stops.

Yue sees it first.

It starts at the temple: a single thread, at first, as fine as spider silk, running back from Mei's hairline through the black. Then another. By the time the lamp burns low, a broad bright streak has bloomed through the dark hair from forehead to nape, white as new snow and gleaming in the tallow light, and Mei, who has not looked up, has no idea.

Hai Ren draws a sharp breath. Kuang lifts his cane and sets it down.

Nobody says a word.

At the sixth hour, Little Mei opens her eyes.

---

"You're all right," Mei says.

She says it again and again, like a prayer, with her forehead pressed to the small damp hand. Little Mei lies against the pillow with her dark eyes half open and her mouth soft with sleep. She is still very pale. But the cold has gone out of her, and her breath moves in and out, slow and sure, and when Kuang puts a warm finger to her wrist he nods once and turns his face away.

"A good pulse," he says gruffly.

"Is it the fault?" Yue asks.

"The fault is there." He clears his throat. "It will always be there. But it is closed. Whatever the Ring did, whatever she gave and the girl gave back, it has set like a bone. I do not think it will open again, if she does not."

"If she does not lend."

"If she does not lend." He looks at the child with a curious, tender, exasperated expression, as at a stubborn pupil. "She will have to be taught. She is not malicious. She is only a child who learned too early that she could help."

Yue says nothing.

She is looking at Mei.

The girl has lifted her head at last, and in the guttering light the streak in her hair is blinding. She does not know about it. She is gazing down at Little Mei with a face so naked with relief that Yue has to look away, and the white tumbles through her black like a banner through smoke.

That's a cost, Yue thinks. That's a visible cost.

It is not the first she has seen on this road. It will not be the last.

"Mei," she says, quietly.

"Mm?"

"Come and sit. You need to eat something."

"In a minute."

"Now."

"Yue." Mei's smile is wan and wide and fierce. "She's alive."

Yue's throat does something painful.

"I know," she says. "Eat."

---

The Sect's embassy is waiting in the courtyard.

Tian Mo has done what she asked. For three days, the forty riders in pale blue have waited outside the lower gate, then in the courtyard, then, when the quarantine story wore thin, on a row of benches in the cold with a kettle of tea and a very polite young guard who answered every question with I will ask. They have been remarkably patient. Yue, who has spent twenty years reading the patience of armed men, thinks it is the most dangerous thing she has ever seen.

Their leader is a man of fifty, lean and gray and upright, in a blue robe with white cloud embroidery on the cuffs. He rises as she crosses the courtyard. He bows. It is a perfect bow, correct to the finger-width, and the smile that accompanies it does not reach his eyes.

"Madam Yue," he says. "I am Chao Wen. Second Elder of the Azure Cloud Sect. I am told you speak for the Hall."

"I speak for the Nine."

"Ah." His gaze is mild. "A smaller company than I expected."

"We are a small company."

"Yet you hold a Roll of two thousand, and a Hall, and a wall." He lets the words lie between them. "I am a plain man, Madam. I will not waste your time. Six of our pupils were sent to the Wall at the turn of the season. I was told they arrived. I was told they climbed to the Seventh Terrace of the Road of Nine, with our Elder Ye, on a matter of the Sect's business. They have not returned. Elder Ye has not returned." The smile does not change. "I would like to know where my people are."

"I don't know," Yue says.

"You don't know."

"Elder Ye went up. That's what I've been told. Your pupils—" She hesitates. She hears the bright small sound of her own pulse. "Your pupils are alive, Elder Chao. One of them, at least, is walking."

He goes very still.

"One," he says.

"The others are asleep." She chooses the word with care. "They'll wake. I can't tell you when. I can tell you it isn't a thing that can be forced, and it isn't a thing you can help by sending forty riders to a quarantined Hall."

"And the one who is walking?"

"Is coming down."

"Down."

"From the Terrace. By the Hundred Stairs." She meets his gaze. "I would expect her at your gate within the week. With a child. Treat them both kindly. I'll hold you to it."

For a long moment, Chao Wen studies her.

She feels the weight of his regard like the weight of a hand. He is quick; she can see it. He is quick, and cautious, and he has already guessed a good deal more than she meant to say. His eyes flick to the pale blue riders on the benches, then back to her face, and something in the set of his jaw eases a fraction.

"You are an honest woman," he says.

"I'm an exhausted one."

"The two are not exclusive." He bows again, and this time the smile is nearly real. "I will wait at the Hundred Stairs, then, Madam. I will see that no one troubles them. And I will tell the Sect what you have told me." A pause. "I hope, for your sake, that it is the truth."

"So do I," says Yue.

---

That night, she goes up to the roof.

It is a small flat roof, reached by a ladder from the east annex, and she has taken to climbing it when the Hall becomes too full of voices. Tonight the sky is clear. The stars are cold and enormous. Far to the north, along the line of the Wall, a thin glow marks the place where the tower stands, and she looks at it for a long time without moving.

"I thought I'd find you here."

Mei has climbed up behind her, with a blanket around her shoulders. She has found a strip of cloth somewhere and bound her hair back, and the white streak still gleams beneath it. She sits down on the stone with a small grunt, like an old woman, and draws her knees up.

"She's asleep," she says. "Kuang is sitting with her. He says if I come back before dawn he'll throw his cane."

"He would, too."

"Mm."

They sit in silence.

After a while Mei says, "Do you want to know what I felt? When I gave it back?"

"If you want to tell me."

"It wasn't what I expected. I thought it would feel like losing something." Her breath makes a small cloud. "It felt like being forgiven. I know that's a strange word. But that's what it was. As though the Ring had been holding something against me, all this time. Some small account I hadn't paid. And when it let go, it let go of that too."

Yue says nothing.

"Do you think that's what it was?" Mei asks. "For Jian? Do you think that's why it cut him loose?"

"I think the Ring is a machine."

"You think it can't forgive."

"I think it does what it's built to do." Yue looks at the glow on the horizon. "But I think the people inside it can. And I think they did."

Mei turns her head.

"I'm going to go after him," Yue says.

It comes out quite simply. She hasn't planned it. She has been carrying it for four days, in the base of her skull, like a stone, and now it is out in the cold air and she finds she is not surprised. "Up the Road. To the Orchard. Whatever's there. I'm not going to stand in a Hall and count sleepers while he climbs alone."

"You can't. It's forty to one."

"I know."

"Eighty years, Yue."

"I know." She has the arithmetic ready. She has, she supposes, been ready for it for a long time. "He took the sitting. That's what the Wall's tower says. He and Hua are under a tree, eating hours. By the time they rise, there will be no one left who remembers us. I'd rather be there when it happens."

"You'd be older than the trees."

"I'd be a Nascent Soul cultivator." Yue smiles faintly. "I'm not so far off as you think. I've been at the peak of the Core realm for three years. I've been waiting for the right wall to hit my head against. This is the biggest I've ever seen."

"And the Hall? The Roll? Kuang?"

"Kuang is an old man with a better memory than I'll ever have. Hai Ren can run the Roll. You can run the Nine." She takes a breath. "And Little Mei needs you. She doesn't need me. I'm no good with children."

"You're good with Little Mei."

"Don't."

"You are, Yue."

"Don't," says Yue. And then, more quietly: "I'll come back. If I can. I give you my word."

Mei looks at her for a long time. The stars shine in her eyes. Then she reaches out and takes Yue's hand, in the blanket, in the cold, and holds it hard.

"Not without a plan," she says.

"I have a plan."

"What is it?"

"I'm going to ask the Sect," says Yue, "for their map."

---

Pebble is waiting at the foot of the roof ladder.

He has been waiting a long time. Yue can tell by the way he stands, with his feet planted a shoulder-width apart and his hands knotted behind him, like a boy who has been told not to move and intends to obey to the letter. He is seventeen, lean as a rake, with a shaven head and a plain gray tunic two sizes too large. He has attached himself to the Nine in the way of a stray who has decided on a house, and no one has had the heart to send him off.

"Master Yue," he says.

"I'm not your master."

"No, Master." His jaw is set. "I heard you on the roof."

She closes her eyes.

"You've been eavesdropping."

"I was sitting. The ladder carries." His voice is level, but she sees his throat work. "You said you're going up the Road. I'd like to come."

"No."

"I'm not asking you to take me to the top. I'd stop wherever you said. I'd sit under whatever tree you told me. I'd carry whatever you told me to carry." The words are tumbling, now, flat and hurried. "I asked Master Jian, the day after the Mending. He said he couldn't. He said it wasn't a road for—" He stops. "He said the Road was heavy and I was light."

"He was right."

"He was wrong." Pebble looks up. His eyes are a dull dark brown, ringed with sleeplessness, and they hold hers without a flicker. "I'm a Foundation cultivator, Master. I'll be Core in a year. I'm not strong. I know it. But I'm the only person on the Wall who ever stayed. Everybody else left, or died, or was carried off. I stayed. That ought to count for something."

Yue is silent.

She remembers him on the Wall in the third week of the war, holding a torch on a collapsing parapet while the stones fell around him. She remembers him weeping, quietly, behind a granary, when Elder Gu died. She remembers him bringing her tea at four in the morning without being asked and setting it down by her elbow and disappearing, like a good domestic ghost.

"It's eighty years," she says. "For us, if we climb. You'd come down an old man."

"I'd come down a Nascent Soul."

"You'd come down without a family."

"I've no family." He says it plainly, without self-pity, as a man states his height. "My parents were Wall-folk. They died at the second breach. My sister went into the Roll. I don't know if she's among the woken. I've looked at every face in the Hall, and she isn't. I think she said no."

Yue's chest tightens.

"I'm not asking to be brave," Pebble says. "I'm asking to be useful. There's nothing here I can do that Tian Mo can't do better. But up there—" He looks toward the roof. "You'll need someone to carry the water."

"That's not a reason."

"It's the only one I've got."

For a long time, she says nothing.

Then she reaches out and takes the boy's shoulder, and he stiffens as though struck. "Get some sleep," she says. "I'll decide in the morning."

"That's what everyone says."

"I know." She smiles, despite herself. "Go to bed, Pebble."

He goes. At the corner of the corridor he looks back, once, and she lifts a hand, and he nods, and is gone.

She stands in the dark with her palm still warm from his shoulder, and thinks that she has made her decision, and that she hates it.

---

Kuang has the Sect's map on his desk by midnight.

He does not say how he got it. He sits behind the stacks of scrolls with his pens behind his ears and his stained sleeve rolled to the elbow, and when Yue enters he looks up, and sighs, and pushes a rolled strip of pale blue silk across the wood. He has not slept in two days. He looks like a man made of paper and ink and stubbornness.

"I traded a favor for it," he says. "A favor I'd been saving for something grander."

"You didn't have to."

"I know." He peers at her over the lamp. "You are going, then."

"Yes."

"Good." He says it flatly, and her heart gives a small startled turn. "I have been waiting for one of you to say so. I could not bring myself to suggest it. It seemed unkind." He rubs his nose. "But it is a long road, Madam Yue, and a bad one, and I do not like to think of Lin Jian climbing it with only a Warden's girl and a ghost for company."

"A ghost."

"Veyra Thann." He says the name with a curious dry relish. "I have spent three days reading what we have on her. It is not much. A line in the Founders' register. A mention in the Wall's first roll. The Wall called her the Keystone Before. And then the rolls go quiet, as if someone had taken a wet cloth and rubbed the name away."

"Rubbed away by whom?"

"By the Stair-Father." Kuang taps the table. "Orrin Thann. Her husband. Who sat at the top of the Seam and told his people for six hundred years that he was alone." He picks up the silk and unrolls it. "You may want to ask him about that."

Yue bends over the map.

It is a fine thing, delicate and precise, with the Hundred Stairs drawn as a thin white thread from the foot of the Azure Cloud Sect's cliffs to the Quay of Bells. Beyond the Quay, a blank. She puts her finger on the blank.

"The Fourth Terrace," she says. "It's not marked."

"No."

"Why not?"

"The Sect's map stops at the Quay. The Sect has never gone further than the Quay. Ye Shuhan was the first, in two hundred years." Kuang looks at her with his reddened eyes. "They think the Road is a stair to heaven. They think it ends in ascension. They have been sending their best pupils up it for six centuries, and not one has come back."

"Not one."

"Until Mo Yan and the girl."

Yue lifts her head.

"They'll come to us, you know," Kuang says. "The Sect. Once they know what the child carries. They will want it. They will say it is a holy relic. They will say it belongs in the Sect's keeping." His thin mouth twists. "They will be wrong, and polite, and numerous."

"Then we'll be wrong, and polite, and faster."

"That," says Kuang, with the ghost of a smile, "is the best thing anyone has said to me all week."

---

A messenger arrives before dawn.

It is a boy in pale blue, on a lathered horse, who has ridden through the night from the Hundred Stairs. He stumbles into the courtyard with his chest heaving and his hands raw and gabbles something so fast that Tian Mo, who meets him at the gate, has to ask him twice to slow down.

When he does, Tian Mo says nothing for a moment.

Then he crosses the courtyard at a run, through the sleeping Hall, up the stair, to the east alcove, where Mei is asleep with her head on the edge of Little Mei's bed. He puts his hand on her shoulder. She wakes with a gasp.

"They've come down," he says.

"Who?"

"A girl of fifteen in a blue robe. And a child." His scarred face is pale. "She's carrying something in her cloak. A bell, the boy says. A white one. And she won't let anyone near her."

Mei stares at him.

"She's asking for the Wall," Tian Mo says. "And she keeps saying one thing, over and over, in a voice that sounds like it's about to break."

"What?"

"Don't let it have her," says Tian Mo. "Please don't let it have her."
